blocks.en_title: 导读
blocks.src:
> 本导读整理自 Socratopia 网站本书介绍页：https://www.socratopia.app/library/close-reading-epic-tragedy-en

Most guides to the classics tell you what happens in the Iliad or Oedipus or the Inferno , and why they matter. This book does something narrower and harder: it teaches you to read them — to open the text yourself, in whatever translation you have to hand, and actually hear how ten lines work. It never asks you to take its word that these works are great. It builds the reading in front of you, line by line, and then hands you the tools to do it alone.

Its method is close reading, and it is relentless about the one thing the genre usually fakes: every quotation is a real, exactly-sourced, public-domain text with its translator named — no invented lines, no borrowed modern renderings, and where scholars genuinely disagree (was Achilles' choice heroic or resigned? is Antigone or Creon the tragedy's center? is Dante's pity to be trusted?), the debate is laid out with the evidence for each side and left open. Along the way it builds a portable vocabulary of the untranslatable words that carry these worlds — mênis (a god-sized wrath, not "anger"), kleos (the glory-in-song a hero trades his life into , not "fame"), nostos (homecoming with the ache of longing folded in), contrapasso (the punishment that is the sin, seen truly) — words English has no equivalents for, carried whole instead of flattened.

The surprises are everywhere once you read closely. Homer's Iliad opens on a single word, "wrath," and its subject turns out to be not the Trojan War but a quarrel inside the Greek camp. Offered immortality by a goddess who loves him, Odysseus says no, and weeps for years, because he would rather go home to a mortal wife and die there. Dante invents for Ulysses a fate Homer never told — a last voyage on which he forsakes his homecoming entirely for the hunger to know — and then, on his own forbidden journey through the afterlife, half-suspects he is looking at a mirror. And running under all of it is one guiding question: how does a text made long ago — up to twenty-five centuries — still read us ? The answer this book earns, three times over, is that a great old work is strange on the surface and familiar in the deep, and close reading is the discipline of crossing the strangeness to reach the depth.

This is the anchor volume of a series (Vol. II turns to Shakespeare; Vol. III to the novel), and it is built to be taught : alongside the prose, every chapter carries Socratic dialogue seeds — question-chains designed to walk you to a reading yourself — which is why it works so well with a companion who asks rather than lectures.

**Target audience**：thoughtful lovers of literature — able high-schoolers, undergraduates, and adult readers. No prerequisites; no Greek or Italian assumed; every technical term (epithet, meter, terza rima, hamartia, peripeteia, anagnorisis, contrapasso, allegory) is explained in plain words at first use. You need only a willingness to reread a passage and stop to think.

**Prerequisites**：none.

**Study hours**：~30–40 hours (26 self-contained chapters across Homer, Greek tragedy, and Dante).

blocks.en_title: Introduction
blocks.src:
This is a book about _reading_ , not about literature. The difference is everything.

There are many fine books that will tell you what happens in the _Iliad_ , why _Oedipus_ matters, what the _Inferno_ means. This is not one of them. This book has a narrower and more demanding aim: to make you a **close reader** of the founding works of Western literature, so that when you open the _Iliad_ or _Oedipus_ or the _Inferno_ yourself, tonight, in whatever translation you have to hand, you can actually _hear_ it, the pressure inside a single Homeric simile, the exact turn where a tragedy reverses, the terrible justice of a punishment in Dante's Hell. Not a summary of the reading, but the training that lets you do the reading, and reach your own.

**What "close reading" means here.** It means starting at the text, in a real, quoted passage, and reading it down to the grain: the exact word, the image and how it turns, the structure, the irony, the sound (even what survives translation), and saying not just "how vivid" but _what it means and why_ , with the door left open where another reader would hear it differently. Every chapter delivers at least one such fully worked reading, built in front of you, step by step, the way a good teacher shows every move rather than announcing a conclusion.

**Three things this book will build in you.** First, a **map of the untranslatable words** that carry these works, _mênis_ , _kleos_ , _nostos_ , _hamartia_ , _contrapasso_ , and more, each carried whole rather than flattened to a misleading English synonym, because a single word carried wrongly can quietly reprogram how you read an entire book. Second, the habit of **reading in translation honestly** : since almost all of us meet these works in someone's English, and every translation is a set of choices, the poem in another language is always plural, and comparing translations is not a scholar's chore but the reader's sharpest tool. Third, and underneath everything, two disciplines: **honesty** about what you actually see on the page, and the **refusal to flatten** a genuine debate into a comfortable verdict, so that where a question is truly open (is Oedipus guilty? is Antigone or Creon right? is Dante's pity to be trusted?), you learn to hold both sides at full strength rather than seize the easy answer.

**Who this is for.** A thoughtful lover of literature, an able high-schooler, an undergraduate, an adult reader, with no prerequisites and no Greek or Italian assumed, but willing to reread a passage and stop to think. Every technical term is explained in plain words at first use. The works are difficult, and this book does not pretend otherwise; where a passage rewards a slow, hard reading, it gets one.

blocks.en_title: Introduction
blocks.src:
**How the book is built.** It moves through three arts in turn, Homer's epic (the _Iliad_ and _Odyssey_), Greek tragedy (Sophocles, Aeschylus, Euripides), and Dante's _Inferno_ , each with its own gap to cross: of time and language with Homer, of a lost theater with tragedy, of unshared belief with Dante. Each chapter is self-contained: a worked close reading, a key-word file where an untranslatable appears, and a set of **Socratic dialogue seeds** , chains of questions designed to lead a reader to notice, and reach, a reading for herself. A note on those seeds and the exercises: this book is read by the Socratopia companion, an AI tutor that teaches you through dialogue, so the exercises' full analyses are written out on purpose, for the tutor to draw on, rather than hidden. A quotation discipline runs throughout, and it is this book's lifeline: every quoted line is a real, accurate, public-domain text with an exact source, and every translation is named; nothing is invented, and where scholarship genuinely disputes a reading, the dispute is flagged as a dispute.

**How to get the most from it.** Read slowly. Reread the quoted passages before you read the analysis of them, and try the reading yourself first. Do the Socratic seeds aloud, or in your head, before looking at where they lead. And when you finish a chapter, or the book, do the thing it is all for: open one of these works and read ten lines with everything you now know. The works themselves are better than any book about them, including this one. The whole purpose of this volume is to hand you back the reading, as your own.

This is the anchor volume of a series. Volume II turns to Shakespeare; Volume III, to the novel. But each stands alone, and this one begins where Western literature begins, with a single word of wrath, and a goddess asked to sing.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: How an Epic Opens: The First Word
blocks.src:
A poem this old does not clear its throat. The oldest surviving long poem of the Western tradition, some twenty-five centuries of readers deep, begins by naming, in a single word, the thing it is about, and then asks a goddess to sing it. Before there is a plot, before there is a hero we can see, before we know we are in a war, there is one word set down like a stone in the road, and everything after it is arranged around that word.

So let us begin where the poem begins, and read the opening as an act of design, not a formality. If we can learn to read the first line of the _Iliad_ closely, we will have most of what we need to read the rest, because a great opening is a compressed version of the whole. This is the first thing close reading asks of you: do not skim the threshold to get to the room. The threshold is built.

Here is the _Iliad_ 's opening, in Alexander Pope's translation of 1715 (Pope died in 1744; his version is centuries out of copyright, and we will meet it often):

> Achilles' wrath, to Greece the direful spring Of woes unnumber'd, heavenly goddess, sing!

Read it once for the sound. Then read it again and watch where the poet has placed each thing.


### 1.1 The first word does the work

In the original Greek, the very first word of the poem, before "Achilles," before "sing," before "goddess," is **mênis** : wrath. Homer does not warm up to his subject. He states it, and states it first, in the emphatic front position that Greek grammar reserves for the thing that matters most. Everything that follows across some twenty-four books is the unfolding of that one word.

Pope, writing in English couplets, cannot put the word first in quite the same way, so watch what he does instead. He gives us "Achilles' wrath" as the very first phrase, and he yokes the wrath immediately to its consequence: it is "to Greece the direful spring / Of woes unnumber'd." A "spring" here is a source, a wellspring, the place a river starts. So in two lines Pope has told you the poem's entire causal engine: one man's anger is the source from which countless griefs flow to his own side. Not the enemy's grief. Greece's. The Greeks are Achilles' own army.

Now compare the plainer prose of Samuel Butler, whose 1898 translation trades Pope's music for clarity (Butler died in 1902; also long in the public domain):

> Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans.

Butler keeps the Greek word order more visibly. The sentence's grammatical object, the thing sung, arrives at once: the anger. And Butler makes explicit what Pope compressed into "to Greece": the anger "brought countless ills upon the Achaeans," the Achaeans being Homer's usual name for the Greeks. Two translations, one fact laid bare: the poem announces that it is about an anger, and that this anger wounds the angry man's own people.

Stop and feel how strange that is. We are about to read the greatest war poem ever written, a poem set in the tenth year of the siege of Troy, and its subject is not the war between Greeks and Trojans. Its subject is a quarrel inside the Greek camp, and the damage one Greek's rage does to other Greeks. The Trojan War is the setting. The wrath is the poem.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: How an Epic Opens: The First Word
blocks.src:
#### Definition: Epic

An **epic** is a long narrative poem, told in an elevated style, about the deeds of heroes and the fate of a people or a world. The ancient Greek epics, the _Iliad_ and the _Odyssey_ , were composed to be performed aloud, sung or chanted by a poet before an audience.

In plain language: an epic is a very long poem about big things (war, homecoming, the founding or falling of a people) told in a grand voice and, at the start, made to be _heard_ , not read silently. Knowing it was heard changes how we read it, as we will see.


### 1.2 "Sing, goddess": who is really speaking?

Look again at what the poet asks. He does not say "I will now tell you about the wrath of Achilles." He commands a goddess to sing it: "heavenly goddess, sing" (Pope), "Sing, O goddess" (Butler). The goddess is a Muse, one of the divine daughters of Memory whom Greek poets invoke as the true source of song. The poet presents himself not as the author but as the mouth: the Muse knows the story, having been there; the poet only relays it.


#### Definition: Invocation of the Muse

An **invocation** is a formal opening appeal to a Muse (a goddess of poetry and memory) to inspire and authorize the song. It became a convention of epic: the poem begins by asking the divine source to sing _through_ the poet.

Why open this way? Read it as a claim about knowledge. The events are vast and old, farther back than any living memory, and the poet is asserting that what you are about to hear is not his invention but something recovered from a source that does not forget. It is the ancient equivalent of a guarantee: this is true, because I did not make it up; a goddess is singing it. Hold onto that gesture. When we reach the tragedians and then Dante, we will watch each of them handle, in his own way, the same problem: by what authority does this voice tell you this story? Homer's answer is the boldest and the simplest. He steps aside and lets a goddess speak.

There is a second, quieter effect. Because the poet asks the Muse to sing, the poem's first verb is an imperative addressed to a god, and the poem's first grammatical _subject_ is that god, not the poet and not Achilles. The human hero, when he arrives, arrives already inside a frame that dwarfs him: gods above, singing; a mortal below, raging; and the rage, for all its size, is a thing the gods can hold in a song and hand to us. That vertical arrangement, gods over mortals, will govern the whole poem.


#### Common Misconception

Many readers assume the invocation is throat-clearing, a pious formula to skip on the way to the action. It is the opposite. The invocation is the poet's first and largest claim: about who knows the story, about why you should trust it, and about the scale (divine above, human below) on which everything will be measured. A reader who skims it has already missed the poem telling her how to read it.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: How an Epic Opens: The First Word
blocks.src:
### 1.3 A word we should not flatten: _mênis_

We said the first word is "wrath." But which wrath? English has a drawer full of near-synonyms (anger, rage, fury, ire, wrath, resentment), and translators reach for different ones. The Greek word Homer chose is not the ordinary word for being angry. It is a special, heavy word, and much of the poem's meaning lives in its heaviness. This is our first encounter with the single most important habit this book will build in you: when a load-bearing word will not cross into English whole, we stop and build a small file on it, so that we never again read it as if it were merely its nearest English synonym.

**Key-word file:_mênis_ (μῆνις)**

* **The word, transliterated:** _mênis_. (The poem's literal first word is _mēnin_ , which is simply _mênis_ in its object form, the form that means "the wrath, as the thing being sung.")
* **Literal sense:** a lasting, sacred, ruinous wrath. In early Greek, _mênis_ is most often used of the anger of _gods_ : a divine, righteous, dangerous anger with the weight of a curse behind it.
* **Why no single English word holds it:** "anger" is far too domestic; we are angry at traffic. "Rage" and "fury" catch the heat but not the sanctity, the sense that this is an anger with cosmic standing, the kind of wrath a god feels. The startling thing in line 1 is that Homer attaches this god-sized word to a _man_ , Achilles. The poem's opening gesture is to give a mortal an anger usually reserved for the divine.
* **How the public-domain translators render it:** Pope, "wrath"; Butler, "anger." Both are defensible; neither can carry the divine coloring by itself. Pope's grander "wrath" comes closer than Butler's plainer "anger," which is one reason to keep more than one translation open (a habit we build in Chapter 9).
* **Do not flatten it to:** ordinary "anger." When you read "the anger of Achilles," silently restore the weight: _the god-like, ruinous, sacred wrath of Achilles_. The whole poem is the story of what such an anger, placed in a human chest, does to the man and to everyone near him.

Once you carry _mênis_ correctly, the opening sharpens. The poem is not about a sulking soldier. It is about a mortal seized by an anger of divine magnitude, an anger the poet marks, by his very first word, as the most dangerous force in the book, more dangerous than the Trojans, more dangerous than the war.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: How an Epic Opens: The First Word
blocks.src:
### 1.4 A first worked reading: the shape of two lines

Let me now do, slowly and in full, the kind of reading this whole book is training you to do on your own. We will take Pope's two lines and read them down to the grain, noticing, and saying _why_ each notice means something, and leaving the door open where another reader would hear it differently.

> Achilles' wrath, to Greece the direful spring Of woes unnumber'd, heavenly goddess, sing!

**First notice: the delayed verb.** The command "sing" does not arrive until the very end, after a two-line sentence has already unrolled the wrath and its consequences. Pope has made you wait for the verb, and in the waiting he has made you hold "Achilles' wrath" and "woes unnumber'd" in suspense, unresolved, until the goddess is finally told to sing them. The syntax enacts a small version of the poem's method: consequence first, cause named, resolution withheld. Why does this matter? Because it teaches you, in the first breath, that this poet controls your attention deliberately; he is not narrating in the order things happened, he is arranging them for effect.

**Second notice: "direful spring."** A "spring" is a gentle word, water rising clean from the ground, the start of a river, the start of a season. Pope hangs "direful" (dreadful, disastrous) on that gentle word, and the collision is the point. The most natural, life-giving image, a spring, is made the source of "woes unnumber'd." Read closely, the line says: from one man's anger, as inevitably as a river from its source, flows an uncountable amount of grief. The metaphor does moral work. It makes the griefs feel not accidental but _sourced_ , flowing by nature from a single origin, the way water must flow downhill.

**Third notice: "to Greece."** We have said this already, but feel it land now. The direful spring flows "to Greece," to Achilles' own side. Pope could have written "to Troy." He wrote "to Greece," faithfully, because that is the poem's shocking truth: the first and worst victims of Achilles' wrath are his own comrades. Here is where a second reader might pause and push back, and we should let her. One might say: is not this simply the plot, that Achilles withdraws and the Greeks suffer? Yes, but notice _how early_ the poem tells you the plot's meaning. It does not let the withdrawal come as a surprise many books in. It tells you on line 1 that this is a poem about self-inflicted, in-group catastrophe, and asks you to watch it happen knowing the end. That knowledge, given up front, is not a spoiler; it is the tragic frame. (When we reach Sophocles in Chapter 11, we will find that this is exactly how tragedy works: you are told the end, and made to watch the characters walk toward it.)

**Where the reading stays open:** what we have _not_ settled is how we are meant to feel about Achilles' wrath. Is it monstrous, a childish tantrum with a body count? Is it, in some sense, justified, the response of a great man to a genuine dishonor? The opening does not say. It names the wrath, sources the griefs to it, and hands the whole matter to us. A poem that wanted to condemn Achilles could have called the wrath "wicked"; a poem that wanted to excuse him could have called it "righteous." Homer calls it _mênis_ , a word that is both terrible and grand, and lets us argue. We will argue, in Chapter 3, when Achilles reasons aloud about why he fights at all.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: How an Epic Opens: The First Word
blocks.src:
That is a close reading: not "note the vivid opening," but a followable walk from the words to a defended meaning, with the alternative left standing.


### 1.5 One poem, and its twin

A last thing to carry forward. The _Iliad_ is one of two great poems that come down to us under Homer's name. Its twin, the _Odyssey_ , opens the same way, with an invocation, but listen to its first word. Where the _Iliad_ begins with _mênis_ , wrath, the _Odyssey_ begins with _andra_ : "man." Butler's version:

> Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy.

The _Iliad_ opens by naming a passion; the _Odyssey_ opens by naming a person, and not just any person but an "ingenious" one, a man of many turns. Already, from two first words, the two poems declare different subjects: one is about an anger, the other about a man's mind and his long way home. We will spend Chapters 3 through 8 letting that contrast unfold, because it turns out to be the deepest thing in Homer: two kinds of hero, two kinds of greatness, set side by side for us to weigh.

And whether the same poet made both is one of the oldest questions in literature. Scholars call it the **Homeric Question** : whether "Homer" was one person or many, whether one hand shaped the _Iliad_ and another the _Odyssey_ , whether the poems were composed in writing or built up over generations of oral performance and only later written down. It is genuinely unsettled, and we will treat it as unsettled. A close reader does not need the question answered to read the lines; but she should know it is open, and never pretend a guess is a fact. That honesty, saying plainly what is known and what is disputed, is the second habit this book will build, right alongside the key-word file.


### 1.X Exercises

_A note on form: this is a literature book, so its exercises are close-reading and discussion prompts, not the Concept-Check / Application / Think-Deeper ladder used in STEM books. Each prompt is followed immediately by its worked reading or discussion, so the Socratopia companion sees prompt and model reading in the same window. The**Socratic Dialogue Seeds** are the primary handoff to the tutor._

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: How an Epic Opens: The First Word
blocks.src:
#### Close-Reading Prompts

**Q1.** Read only the first phrase of each poem: the _Iliad_ 's "Achilles' wrath" (Pope) and the _Odyssey_ 's "that ingenious hero" (Butler). Without knowing anything else, what does each poem promise to be about, and how do the two promises differ?

Hint

One phrase names an emotion; the other names a person and gives him a single adjective. What kind of story follows from "a wrath"? What kind follows from "an ingenious man"?

**Answer:** The _Iliad_ promises a poem organized around a passion: a wrath will be the through-line, and we should expect the story to trace that anger's course, its cause, its damage, its end. The _Odyssey_ promises a poem organized around a _person_ defined by a quality: ingenuity, cunning, resourcefulness. So we should expect a story of problems solved by wit, of a mind making its way. The difference is between a poem whose spine is an emotion (and so a poem that will feel driven, singular, tending toward catastrophe) and a poem whose spine is a character trait (and so a poem that will feel various, episodic, tending toward survival and return). A strong answer notices that Homer has front-loaded each poem's organizing principle into a single opening phrase, so that the openings are not decoration but design.


#### Translation-Comparison Prompt

**Q2.** Here is the _Iliad_ 's opening in Pope and in Butler, side by side:

* Pope: "Achilles' wrath, to Greece the direful spring / Of woes unnumber'd, heavenly goddess, sing!"
* Butler: "Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans."

Name one thing Pope's version gains over Butler's, and one thing Butler's gains over Pope's. Do not say one is "better"; say what each _does_.

Hint

Think about music versus information. Which version could be sung? Which tells you more, more plainly, about who Achilles is and who suffers?

**Answer:** Pope gains music and compression: the rhymed couplet, the drum of "woes unnumber'd," the grand collision of "direful spring." It sounds like an epic; it has the elevation the Greek surely had. But Pope pays for it in plainness. Butler gains clarity and information: he tells us Achilles is "son of Peleus" (a fact Pope's readers were expected to know), and he names "the Achaeans" outright, so a first-time reader knows exactly who suffers. Butler reads like accurate prose; Pope reads like a poem. Neither is "the _Iliad_ "; each is a choice about what to save when you cannot save everything, and the truth of Homer's opening is somewhere in the space between them. A strong answer resists ranking them and instead names the trade each translator made: Pope trades information for music, Butler trades music for information. (This is the whole method of Chapter 9, previewed here.)

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: How an Epic Opens: The First Word
blocks.src:
#### Key-Word Prompt

**Q3.** Given the key-word file for _mênis_ above, rewrite this flat sentence so that it restores the word's real weight: "The poem is about Achilles being angry that his prize was taken."

**Answer:** Something like: "The poem is about a _mênis_ in Achilles, a wrath of the size and heat a god feels, kindled when his honor was stripped from him." The point of the exercise is to feel how much the flat sentence loses. "Being angry that his prize was taken" makes Achilles sound petty and small; restoring _mênis_ makes him sound seized by something vast and dangerous. Both readings are available in the poem, and the tension between them (is this pettiness or grandeur?) is exactly what Homer leaves open. A strong rewrite keeps the divine scale of the word without deciding, yet, whether Achilles deserves it. The criteria for a strong answer: it lifts "angry" to something with sacred weight, and it does not secretly settle the open question of whether the wrath is justified.


#### Socratic Dialogue Seeds (primary handoff)

These are chains the companion can walk the learner through. Each notes where readers typically stall and how the tutor can press.

**Seed A — the delayed verb.** Start: "Where in Pope's two lines does the command 'sing' finally appear?" (Learner locates it at the very end.) Then: "Why might the poet make us wait for it?" _Common stall:_ the learner says "for emphasis" and stops. _Tutor move:_ accept it, then push: "Emphasis on what, exactly? What are we forced to hold in mind while we wait for the verb?" Guide toward the idea that the syntax makes us hold the wrath and the woes in suspense, so the poem's arrangement (consequence, then cause, then release) is felt in the very grammar. End by asking: "So is Homer telling us the story in the order it happened, or in an order he designed? What does that tell you about how to read the rest?"

**Seed B — the god-sized word in a human chest.** Start: "The word _mênis_ is usually used for the anger of gods. Homer uses it here for a man. What is surprising about that?" _Common stall:_ the learner treats it as just a big synonym for "angry." _Tutor move:_ offer the contrast directly: "If I said your anger at a rude driver was _mênis_ , would that fit? Why not?" Draw out that _mênis_ has sanctity and cosmic weight, not just heat. Then the real question: "If the poem gives a man an anger the size of a god's, is it telling us Achilles is grand, or that he is dangerous, or both? Find one word in the opening that supports each reading." (This opens the Chapter 3 debate.)

**Seed C — whose grief?** Start: "The wrath brings 'woes unnumber'd' to _Greece_ , Achilles' own side. Were you expecting the poem to say Troy?" _Common stall:_ the learner knows the plot and answers mechanically ("because he withdraws from battle"). _Tutor move:_ redirect from plot to design: "Yes, but why does the _poem_ tell us this on line 1, before any of that has happened? What does it do to how we watch the story, to know from the start that the hero's anger will wound his friends?" Guide toward the tragic frame: we are made to watch a catastrophe we have been warned of, which is exactly the pressure a close reader learns to feel.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: How an Epic Opens: The First Word
blocks.src:
#### Open Reading Note

**Q4.** By the end of the poem, Achilles' wrath will have shifted its target and, in the final book, softened into something like pity (we will read that scene in Chapter 8). Write a few sentences on this question, giving your strongest reading _and_ your strongest counter-reading: **Does the opening word _mênis_ condemn Achilles, or simply name him?** There is no single right answer; a strong response builds both sides from the text.

**Discussion:** One strong reading: _mênis_ names without condemning. The word is grand as well as terrible; Homer never calls the wrath wicked; he sources catastrophe to it but also builds the whole poem's dignity on the man who feels it. On this view the opening is diagnostic, not moral: here is the force we will study. The strongest counter-reading: to source "woes unnumber'd" to the wrath _is_ a kind of judgment; a poem that opens by tallying the innocent dead a passion caused has already tilted us against that passion, however grand. A serious reader might land anywhere between, and the best responses will notice that Homer seems deliberately to have built the ambiguity: he chose a word that is both sacred and ruinous, and he refused the adjectives ("wicked," "righteous") that would have closed the case. The companion should reward the learner for holding both readings at once rather than picking a side too fast; the criterion for a strong reading here is that it can state the _other_ side persuasively.


### Chapter Summary

We read the _Iliad_ 's opening as a designed act, not a formality. The poem names its subject in its first word, _mênis_ , a sacred and ruinous wrath usually reserved for gods, and by placing it first it makes an anger, not the Trojan War, the true subject of the poem. The invocation of the Muse ("Sing, goddess") is the poet's claim about authority and scale: the story comes from a source that does not forget, and it will be measured on a vertical from gods above to mortals below. We built our first key-word file, on _mênis_ , establishing the book's central habit: when a word will not cross into English whole, we stop and carry it correctly rather than flatten it to its nearest synonym. And we met the book's other governing habit, honesty about what is settled and what is open, in the Homeric Question, which we will leave unsettled because it is unsettled.

Two threads begin here and will run through the whole book. **Thread 1** , our guiding question, is whether and how a text two and a half thousand years old can still read _us_ , and how we read closely enough to hear it across the double gap of time and language; the _mênis_ we had to reconstruct is that gap in miniature. **Thread 2** , the key-word map, opens with _mênis_ and will grow, word by word, into a portable vocabulary for these works. In Chapter 2 we turn from the first word to the poem's signature engine, the Homeric simile, and read a single picture all the way to the bottom.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Homeric Simile: Reading One Picture to the Bottom
blocks.src:
In the last chapter we watched an epic name its subject in a single word. Now we turn to the poem's most characteristic move, the thing that, more than any other, makes reading Homer feel like reading Homer. It is the extended simile: the moment when the poet stops the battle, opens a window, and shows us something from a wholly different world, a farmer, a snowfall, a lion, a mother shooing a fly from her sleeping child, and then closes the window and lets the fighting resume.

These similes are so frequent and so beautiful that readers often let them wash by as decoration. That is the mistake this chapter exists to correct. A Homeric simile is not ornament laid over the story; it is a second story told alongside the first, and the two stories comment on each other in ways that carry much of the poem's meaning. So we will do here exactly what the chapter title promises: take one simile and read it all the way to the bottom, until we can say not just "how vivid" but _what it means_ and _why it is placed here_.


### 2.1 What a simile is, and what an epic simile does

Start with the plain machinery.


#### Definition: Simile

A **simile** is a comparison of one thing to another using "like" or "as": _her courage was like a fire_. It differs from a metaphor (which says one thing _is_ another: _her courage was a fire_) in keeping the two things visibly separate, held apart by the word "like."

Every simile has two parts, and it helps to have names for them. The thing being described (here, the courage) is the **tenor**. The thing it is compared to (the fire) is the **vehicle**. In an ordinary simile the vehicle is brief: "quick as a hare," and we move on. The vehicle exists only to illuminate the tenor, and once it has done its one job it is spent.

The Homeric or **epic simile** is different in scale, and the difference is the whole point.


#### Definition: Epic Simile (Homeric Simile)

An **epic simile** is an extended comparison, often running several lines, in which the vehicle (the thing compared _to_) is developed at such length and with such independent detail that it becomes a small scene in its own right, temporarily pulling the reader out of the main narrative.

In plain language: it is a simile that grows a whole little world. Homer says the warriors fell upon each other "like" wolves, and then keeps describing the wolves, their hunger, their bloody muzzles, the lamb they are tearing, until for a few lines we have left the battlefield entirely and are standing on a hillside among the wolves. Then he returns us. The art is in what those extra, "unnecessary" lines do, and they are never unnecessary.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Homeric Simile: Reading One Picture to the Bottom
blocks.src:
### 2.2 The worked reading: the generations of leaves

Let us take a single famous simile and read it all the way down. It comes in Book 6 of the _Iliad_. On the battlefield, two warriors from opposing sides, the Greek Diomedes and the Lycian Glaucus, meet between the lines. Before they fight, Diomedes asks who Glaucus is, and Glaucus answers with a comparison that has echoed for twenty-five centuries. Here it is first in Pope's couplets:

> Like leaves on trees the race of man is found, Now green in youth, now withering on the ground; Another race the following spring supplies; They fall successive, and successive rise.

And here is the same passage in Butler's plain prose:

> Men come and go as leaves year by year upon the trees. … Even so is it with the generations of mankind, the new spring up as the old are passing away.

(Remember it is _Glaucus_ speaking, not the narrator; Butler's rendering runs on between these two sentences, with a line on the autumn wind and the returning spring, and we quote the framing sentences that carry the point.)

Now let us read.

**First notice: who says it, and when.** This is not the narrator's simile; it is _Glaucus's_ , spoken by a man about to risk his life, in answer to "who are you?" His reply amounts to: _why does it matter who I am? Men are leaves._ So the simile is characterized before we even weigh its content: it is the philosophy of a soldier facing death, a way of making his own possible death bearable by dissolving it into a natural cycle. Already this is richer than decoration. The comparison tells us something about the speaker's state of mind.

**Second notice: the direction of the comparison.** The tenor is the generations of men; the vehicle is leaves. Feel which way the feeling runs. Leaves are humble, countless, and, crucially, _not tragic_ : no one grieves a fallen leaf. By comparing men to leaves, Glaucus borrows the leaf's un-grieved quality and lends it to human death. If men are leaves, then a man's death, like a leaf's fall, is ordinary, seasonal, and nothing to make a fuss about. The simile is doing consolation work, and we can see exactly how: it transfers the emotional temperature of the vehicle (calm, cyclical, un-mourned) onto the tenor (a soldier's death, which we would otherwise mourn).

**Third notice: the turn, and the cost of the consolation.** But read once more and feel the ache underneath the comfort. The same comparison that makes death bearable also makes each individual life small. If you are a leaf, your death does not matter; but neither, quite, does your life. The consolation and the desolation are the same sentence. This is the mark of a great simile: it does not resolve a feeling, it holds two feelings at once. Glaucus reaches for the leaves to steady himself before battle, and the image steadies him precisely by telling him he is nothing special. A close reader does not pick one of these meanings. She names both and sees that Homer has fused them.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Homeric Simile: Reading One Picture to the Bottom
blocks.src:
**Fourth notice: the "reach," where the vehicle outgrows its job.** Here is the feature most special to the Homeric simile, and the thing to train your eye to catch. A minimal simile would have stopped at "men are like leaves." But the picture keeps unfolding: green in youth, withering on the ground, another race supplied in spring, falling and rising in succession. Those extra clauses are not needed to make the basic point (men die, others are born). They are there to let the vehicle become _a whole scene we inhabit_ , a real forest with real seasons, so that when we come back to the battlefield we bring the forest's calm with us. This is what I call the reach of a Homeric simile: the vehicle reaches past its assigned task and acquires a life of its own, and that overflow is where the poetry lives.

Notice, too, what the reach does to _time_. The battle is a single terrible afternoon. The simile opens onto years, onto the endless turning of the seasons, onto all the generations that have fallen and risen. For a few lines the poem lifts us out of this one fight and shows us the vast, patient cycle that contains it and does not care about it. Then it sets us back down, and the fight resumes, and we watch it now with the forest in our eyes. That widening and narrowing of scale, from one man's death to all death and back, is the emotional engine of the whole _Iliad_.


### 2.3 The pattern across the poem: peace lighting up war

Once you can read one simile this way, a larger pattern comes into focus. The _Iliad_ is a poem almost entirely of war, yet its similes are drawn overwhelmingly from _peace_ : farming, herding, weather, cooking, mothers and children, craftsmen at work. A spear-cast is "like" a farmer's irrigation channel breaking loose; a fallen warrior drops "like" a poplar a wheelwright has felled to bend into a wheel; a wound bleeds "as" a woman stains ivory with dye. The battlefield is lit, again and again, by pictures of the ordinary world the fighters have left behind and may never return to.

Read closely, this is not a quirk of style but a sustained argument the poem makes without ever stating it. By showing us the world of peace inside every act of war, the similes keep before us everything the war destroys, and everything the fighters are: not only killers but also, in the world the similes remember, farmers and shepherds and fathers. The similes are the poem's memory of peace, carried into the middle of the killing. You do not need Homer to tell you war is terrible; he shows you a lion, a harvest, a child, at the exact moment a man dies, and lets the contrast do the work.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Homeric Simile: Reading One Picture to the Bottom
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

Readers often treat the Homeric simile as a decorative pause, a bit of pretty scenery before the action resumes, and feel free to skim it. In fact the simile is frequently where the passage's deepest meaning sits. The narrative tells you _what happens_ ; the simile tells you _what it is like to be inside what happens_ , and often _what it costs_. Skimming the similes is like listening to a song and tuning out whenever the music swells: you are skipping precisely the parts the artist worked hardest on.

A second, subtler misconception is that a good simile "matches" its subject neatly, point for point. The best Homeric similes do not match neatly; they leak. The leaves simile is not a tidy diagram of human mortality; it carries an extra freight of feeling (the un-grieved smallness of a leaf) that complicates the very consolation it offers. That leakage is not a flaw. It is the difference between an illustration and a poem.


### 2.4 Why translation matters here too

We read the leaves simile in two English versions, and it is worth pausing on what changed between them, because it previews a habit we will make central in Chapter 9. Pope gives us "successive rise," rhymed and metrical, the cycle turned into a small, closed music that itself sounds like a turning wheel of seasons; the form performs the content. Butler gives us "the new spring up as the old are passing away," plainer, sadder, with none of Pope's consoling music, so that in Butler the _loss_ is more audible and the consolation thinner. Same simile, two different balances of comfort and grief, struck by two translators' different instruments. Neither is wrong. Each is a reading of Homer, made in the act of carrying him across.

Keep this in mind whenever a simile moves you: some of what moves you is Homer, and some of it is the translator's English. The close reader learns to feel, at least roughly, where the seam is. She is never quite reading "Homer"; she is reading a Homer, in someone's English, and the honest pleasure is sharper for knowing it.


### 2.X Exercises

_As in Chapter 1, these are close-reading and discussion prompts with the model reading given immediately after each, and the Socratic dialogue seeds as the primary handoff._


#### Close-Reading Prompts

**Q1.** In the leaves simile, identify the tenor and the vehicle, then explain in one or two sentences how the _feeling_ attached to the vehicle transfers to the tenor.

Hint

The tenor is what is really being talked about; the vehicle is the picture used to talk about it. Ask: what emotions do we normally attach to falling leaves, and what happens when we lend those emotions to human death?

**Answer:** The tenor is the generations of human beings; the vehicle is leaves on a tree through the seasons. The feeling normally attached to leaves is calm and cyclical acceptance: leaves fall every autumn and no one mourns them, because more come in spring. The simile transfers that un-grieved, seasonal calm onto human death, which makes a soldier's death feel ordinary and bearable rather than catastrophic. A strong answer also notices the cost of the transfer: making death un-tragic also makes each life un-special, so the consolation and the sadness arrive in the same image.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Homeric Simile: Reading One Picture to the Bottom
blocks.src:
#### Structure Prompt

**Q2.** A minimal version of Glaucus's point would be just: "men die, and others are born." Homer instead gives us four full lines about green youth, withering, spring, and successive rising and falling. What do those "extra" lines accomplish that the minimal version could not? (This is the "reach" of the epic simile.)

Hint

Think about time and scale. How long a stretch of time does the minimal version cover? How long does the extended version make you feel? Where has the extended version taken you, and what do you bring back when you return to the battlefield?

**Answer:** The extra lines let the vehicle become a scene we inhabit rather than a point we register. By developing the forest through its full seasonal cycle, Homer widens the poem's time-scale from a single deadly afternoon to the endless turning of the years and generations, and he lifts us out of the battle into a vast, patient, indifferent natural order that contains the battle and does not care about it. Then he returns us to the fight, and we watch it now against that immense backdrop. The minimal version delivers information; the extended version delivers an _experience of scale_ , the sudden zoom out and back that is the emotional engine of the _Iliad_. A strong answer names this widening-and-narrowing of scale as the specific effect of the "reach."


#### Translation-Comparison Prompt

**Q3.** Compare "They fall successive, and successive rise" (Pope) with "the new spring up as the old are passing away" (Butler). Which version leans toward consolation, and which toward loss? Point to the specific words that do it.

**Answer:** Pope leans toward consolation. His line is rhymed and balanced, and the repeated "successive … successive" enacts a smooth, reassuring cycle, a wheel that keeps turning; the _music_ itself soothes. Butler leans toward loss. "The old are passing away" is a dying fall, plain and unmusical, with no rhyme to close the wound, so we hear the departure more than the renewal. The tell is in the balance of the clauses: Pope gives falling and rising equal, chiming weight ("fall … rise"), while Butler subordinates the springing-up to the passing-away, ending his sentence on death. A strong answer resists calling either "better" and instead names each as a defensible reading of the same Greek: Pope hears the cycle's comfort, Butler hears its grief, and both are really in Homer.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Homeric Simile: Reading One Picture to the Bottom
blocks.src:
#### Socratic Dialogue Seeds (primary handoff)

**Seed A — catching the reach.** Start: "Read the leaves simile and tell me the shortest sentence that captures its basic point." (Learner offers something like "people die and are replaced.") Then: "Now count how many more words Homer spends after that point is already made. Why doesn't he just stop?" _Common stall:_ the learner says "to make it beautiful" and halts. _Tutor move:_ accept beauty, then press for function: "Beautiful how, and to what end? While you were reading those extra lines, where were you standing, on the battlefield or in the forest? What did you bring back?" Guide to the idea of scale: the reach lifts us into a larger time and lets us return changed.

**Seed B — the double edge.** Start: "Does comparing men to leaves make you feel better or worse about death?" (Learner picks one.) _Tutor move, whichever they pick:_ argue the other side. If they say "better," note that a leaf's life is as un-special as its death; if they say "worse," note the genuine comfort of belonging to a cycle larger than yourself. Aim: get the learner to hold both at once, and to see that Homer built the image to hold both. End: "Is a simile that makes you feel two opposite things at once a failed simile or a great one? Why?"

**Seed C — peace inside war.** Start: "The _Iliad_ is almost all battle, but its similes keep showing us farmers, shepherds, mothers, and children. Why would a war poem be full of pictures of peace?" _Common stall:_ "for contrast." _Tutor move:_ push past the label: "Contrast that does what? What does it keep in front of us at the moment a man is killed?" Guide toward the reading that the similes are the poem's memory of everything war destroys, and its insistence that the men dying are also farmers and fathers. Then: "Does this make the poem anti-war, or is it doing something harder to name?"


#### Open Reading Note

**Q4.** Glaucus reaches for the leaves image to steady himself before a fight he might not survive. Write a few sentences arguing, first, that the simile is genuinely consoling, and then, that it is quietly devastating. Which reading finally persuades you, and can you state the other side fairly?

**Discussion:** The consoling reading: to see yourself as a leaf is to be released from the terror of your own death; you join a cycle that has always turned and always will, and there is real peace in that surrender of self-importance, the peace of the small thing that belongs. The devastating reading: the very move that softens death also empties life of singularity; if your death does not matter, your particular, once-only life does not matter either, and the calm is bought at the price of everything that makes you _you_. The best responses will notice that these are not two separate readings to choose between but one meaning with two faces, and that Homer's refusal to resolve them is the source of the simile's staying power. Whichever side finally persuades the learner, the criterion for a strong reading is the same as in Chapter 1: it can state the opposing reading persuasively, because the poem genuinely supports both.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Homeric Simile: Reading One Picture to the Bottom
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

We took the _Iliad_ 's signature device, the extended or epic simile, and read one example, Glaucus's comparison of the generations of men to leaves (_Iliad_ 6), all the way to the bottom. We learned the working vocabulary (tenor and vehicle), and we learned to watch for the "reach," the way the Homeric vehicle overflows its assigned task and becomes a scene we inhabit, widening the poem's scale from one death to all death and back. We saw that a great simile holds opposite feelings at once (the leaves both console and diminish), and that the _Iliad_ 's similes, drawn overwhelmingly from peace, quietly keep before us everything the war destroys. Finally, comparing Pope and Butler on the same lines, we felt again that "the poem in English is always plural" (Thread 3), a habit we will make a full method in Chapter 9.

This builds directly on Chapter 1: there we learned that Homer designs, that nothing in the opening is accidental; here we learned that the design extends into every simile, that the "decorative" pauses are load-bearing. In Chapter 3 we turn from how Homer writes to what his greatest hero _wants_ , reading Achilles reason aloud, in Book 9, about the value he is trading his life for, a value carried by our next key-word, _kleos_.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Kleos: The Economy of Glory-for-Death
blocks.src:
We have watched Homer name his subject and light his battles with the world of peace. Now we go to the center of the _Iliad_ and ask the question the whole poem circles: what is a hero willing to die for, and why? The answer is a single Greek word, and until you carry that word correctly you cannot understand a line of what Achilles does. So this chapter is built around our second key-word, and around one speech in which the greatest of the Greek heroes stops fighting and _reasons aloud_ about whether fighting is worth it.

That speech is unusual and precious. Homer's heroes mostly act; here, in Book 9 of the _Iliad_ , Achilles sits still and thinks, and lets us hear the arithmetic of his life. To read it closely is to watch an entire heroic culture do its accounting out loud.


### 3.1 The scene: an embassy to a man who has stopped

A reminder of where we are, kept to the minimum the passage needs. Achilles, dishonored by the Greek commander Agamemnon, who seized a war-prize that was rightfully his, has withdrawn from the fighting. Without him the Greeks are losing badly. So Agamemnon sends an embassy, three men, to Achilles' tent with an enormous offer: treasure, land, a marriage, if only Achilles will return to battle. The embassy scene is the emotional hinge of the poem's first half, because it forces Achilles to say, for the first time, what he actually thinks about the whole enterprise.

And what he says is startling. Listen (Butler's prose):

> He that fights fares no better than he that does not; coward and hero are held in equal honour, and death deals like measure to him who works and him who is idle.

Read that slowly. Achilles has noticed something that threatens to unravel the entire warrior code. If the brave man and the coward die alike, and if honor can be stripped from the brave man (as his was) and handed elsewhere, then what exactly is the point of risking your life? The reward that was supposed to make the risk worthwhile, honor, has just been shown to be detachable, arbitrary, something a commander can confiscate. Achilles is doing something no hero is supposed to do: he is auditing the books of heroism, and finding them not to balance.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Kleos: The Economy of Glory-for-Death
blocks.src:
### 3.2 The key word: _kleos_

To feel the force of his crisis, we need the word for the thing he thought he was buying with his life.

**Key-word file:_kleos_ (κλέος)**

* **The word, transliterated:** _kleos_.
* **Literal sense:** "what is heard" of a person, from the verb "to hear." _Kleos_ is the report of you that travels, the glory that is spoken and sung, above all the fame that survives your death in the songs of later people. It is, quite literally, the reason epic poetry exists: the _Iliad_ itself is Achilles' _kleos_ , the song that keeps his name alive.
* **Why no single English word holds it:** "fame" is close but too cheap and too modern; we speak of fame as celebrity, something bought with attention. _Kleos_ is earned only with excellence, usually deadly excellence, and it is imagined as a near-physical substance, a thing you can win, be given, have taken away, and, above all, trade your mortal life _into_. "Glory" catches the grandeur but not the crucial mechanism: that _kleos_ is what is _heard_ , carried on the breath of others, and so depends utterly on there being poets to sing it and audiences to remember. Your _kleos_ lives in other mouths.
* **How the public-domain translators render it:** Pope tends toward "fame" and "glory"; Butler uses "name" ("my name will live for ever"), which nicely catches the survival-of-the-name aspect while losing the "heard, sung" root.
* **Do not flatten it to:** "fame" in the modern celebrity sense. Restore, each time: _the glory that is sung of me and outlives my body._ When Achilles weighs _kleos_ against a long life, he is not choosing between being famous and being obscure; he is choosing between two forms of existence, one that ends in the ground and one that goes on in song.

We need one more small word to read the speech, because Achilles does his reasoning not with a cool "mind" but with something hotter.

**Key-word file:_thumos_ (θυμός)** — a shorter, satellite entry alongside _kleos_.

* **Literal sense:** spirit, the seat of feeling, drive, anger, and appetite; the part of a person that surges, that "wants," that a hero argues with as if it were a companion in his chest.
* **How the public-domain translators render it:** usually "heart," "spirit," or "soul" in Pope and Butler, which catch the surging feeling but blur the fact that in Greek this is where a hero _reasons_ , not merely where he feels.
* **Why it matters here:** when Achilles deliberates, Greek does not locate the decision in a detached intellect. It happens in the _thumos_ , where passion and reasoning are not yet split apart. So his "arithmetic" is never bloodless; it is reasoning done by a whole hot self. Do not flatten _thumos_ to "mind" or "soul."

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Kleos: The Economy of Glory-for-Death
blocks.src:
### 3.3 The worked reading: the two fates

Now the heart of it. Achilles reveals that his mother, the sea-goddess Thetis, has told him he carries two possible destinies, and he must choose between them. Here is his statement of the choice, in Butler:

> If I stay here and fight, I shall not return alive but my name will live for ever: whereas if I go home my name will die, but it will be long ere death shall take me.

Let us read this to the bottom.

**First notice: it is a genuine choice, and a symmetrical one.** Most of us do not know the terms of our death. Achilles does, exactly, and this knowledge is the poem's great gift and burden to him. The two fates are laid out with brutal clarity, and each is total: on one side, death soon plus _kleos_ forever; on the other, life long plus oblivion. There is no third option, no way to have both. Homer has built a perfect machine for exposing what _kleos_ is worth, by pricing it precisely: the price of eternal name is an early grave.

**Second notice: the tenses, and where the "forever" sits.** Look at what lasts in each fate. In the first, the _man_ does not last ("I shall not return alive") but the _name_ does ("will live for ever"). In the second, the man lasts ("it will be long ere death shall take me") but the name dies ("my name will die"). Homer has split a person into two parts, the body and the _kleos_ , and shown that you cannot save both. This is the whole tragic economy of the heroic world in one sentence: glory is bought with life, and the currency does not convert back.

**Third notice: that he is telling us this now, in the moment of refusal.** The context transforms the speech. Achilles lays out the two fates _while explaining why he might just go home_. He is, at this instant, leaning toward the second fate, the long life, the death of his name. And that is astonishing, because it means the greatest warrior in the poem is, for one book, seriously considering trading away the very _kleos_ that his whole identity is built on. The audit of Book 9 has shaken him so badly that immortality-in-song no longer looks obviously worth an early death. A close reader feels the ground move here: the poem is questioning its own highest value, through the mouth of the man who embodies it.

**Where the reading stays open.** Does Achilles' wavering _refute_ the heroic code, or does it deepen it? One reading: Achilles sees through _kleos_ , sees that it is a story other people tell to get young men to die, and for one clear-eyed book he refuses the con. On this view Book 9 is the most modern moment in ancient literature, a hero discovering the emptiness of glory. The opposing reading, equally strong: Achilles does not reject _kleos_ ; he grieves its cost. He wants it to be worth the price and is agonized to find the price so high, and his eventual return to battle (driven, as we will see, by the death of his friend Patroclus) shows that when the choice becomes real he chooses the name after all. On this view Book 9 does not debunk heroism; it makes heroism cost something, so that Achilles' final acceptance of his early death is a true choice and not a reflex. Homer does not tell us which reading is right. He gives us a hero who both sees through glory and finally dies for it, and leaves us to decide whether that is contradiction or wisdom. Hold the question; we will return to it in Chapter 8, when Achilles, having chosen death and glory, meets the father of the man he killed.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Kleos: The Economy of Glory-for-Death
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

Students often read Achilles' choice as "a short glorious life versus a long boring one," as if it were a matter of taste, excitement over comfort. That flattens it. The choice is between two _kinds of immortality-or-not_ : to die into song (to exist forever in the _kleos_ other people carry) or to live long and then vanish utterly. For a Greek without a comforting afterlife, this is not a lifestyle preference; it is the only form of "living forever" on offer, and it can be had only by dying young. Once you see the choice that way, Achilles' hesitation stops looking like cowardice and starts looking like the deepest question the poem can ask: is a name in other people's mouths worth your one actual life?


### 3.4 Why this is the poem's center

Return, now, to the poem's first word, _mênis_. In Chapter 1 we said the _Iliad_ is about an anger. We can now say more precisely what the anger is _about_. Achilles' wrath began when Agamemnon stripped his war-prize, and a modern reader might think: it is only a prize, a woman, some bronze. But in the economy we have just uncovered, the prize is not the point; it is the visible token of _honor_ , and honor is the down-payment on _kleos_. To take Achilles' prize is to say publicly that his excellence does not earn its due, which threatens the entire logic by which he is trading his life for a name. His rage is the rage of a man who has bet everything on one currency and watched someone debase it. That is why the quarrel of Book 1 can carry the weight of twenty-four books: it is not a squabble over loot, it is a crisis in the meaning of a hero's death.

This is the payoff of reading closely for the key word. Carry _kleos_ correctly and the whole poem organizes itself around it: the wrath, the withdrawal, the audit of Book 9, the return, the death Achilles knowingly chooses. Flatten _kleos_ to "fame" and it all shrinks to a sulk about a stolen girl. The word is the poem.


### 3.X Exercises

_Close-reading and discussion prompts, model reading given immediately after each; the Socratic dialogue seeds are the primary handoff._


#### Close-Reading Prompts

**Q1.** In Achilles' statement of his two fates, what survives in each fate, and what perishes? Use the split to explain what _kleos_ is.

Hint

Read for the tenses. In the "stay and fight" fate, what "will live for ever," and what will not? In the "go home" fate, reverse it.

**Answer:** In the "stay and fight" fate, the body perishes ("I shall not return alive") but the name survives ("my name will live for ever"). In the "go home" fate, the body survives long ("it will be long ere death shall take me") but the name perishes ("my name will die"). _Kleos_ is precisely the thing in the first column: the name-that-lives-forever, the sung glory that outlasts the body. The split shows that a person, for Homer, has two parts that can be saved separately but not together: the mortal body and the immortal _kleos_. To choose _kleos_ is to spend the body to save the name. A strong answer names _kleos_ as this survival-in-song and notes that the two fates are a machine for pricing it exactly: the cost of eternal name is an early death.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Kleos: The Economy of Glory-for-Death
blocks.src:
#### Application Problem (connecting to Chapter 1)

**Q2.** In Chapter 1 we said the _Iliad_ 's first word, _mênis_ , names an anger that wounds Achilles' own side. Using this chapter's account of _kleos_ and honor, explain _why_ the loss of a war-prize could enrage Achilles enough to let his own comrades die.

Hint

The prize is a token. A token of what? And what is that thing the down-payment on?

**Answer:** The war-prize is not valuable to Achilles chiefly as property; it is the public token of his honor, the visible sign that his excellence in battle is being given its due. Honor, in turn, is the down-payment on _kleos_ : a hero earns lasting glory by winning honor now, in the recognition of his peers. When Agamemnon seizes the prize, he publicly denies Achilles the honor his excellence has earned, which strikes at the whole logic by which Achilles is trading his life for a name. If honor can be confiscated arbitrarily, then the _kleos_ it was supposed to secure is worthless, and the bargain of the heroic life collapses. So the rage is not greed over loot; it is the fury of a man watching the currency he has staked his death on be debased. This directly connects to Chapter 1: _mênis_ is god-sized precisely because what has been threatened is not a possession but the meaning of Achilles' mortality. A strong answer links prize to honor to _kleos_ to the choice of death, showing the chain.


#### Key-Word Prompt

**Q3.** Rewrite this sentence to restore the weight of _kleos_ : "Achilles chose to be famous instead of living a long life."

**Answer:** Something like: "Achilles chose the glory that would be sung of him forever, at the cost of his one mortal life, over a long life that would end in the total silence of his name." The exercise exposes how much "famous" loses: it makes the choice sound like a bid for celebrity rather than a bid for the only immortality a Greek could imagine. A strong rewrite keeps three things the flat version drops: that _kleos_ is _sung_ (it lives in others' memory), that it is _permanent_ (it outlives the body), and that its alternative is not obscurity-while-alive but _oblivion after death_. The criteria: the rewrite must make the stakes existential, not reputational.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Kleos: The Economy of Glory-for-Death
blocks.src:
#### Socratic Dialogue Seeds (primary handoff)

**Seed A — the audit.** Start: "Achilles says the coward and the hero are 'held in equal honour,' and death takes them both alike. Why is that observation so dangerous to a warrior?" _Common stall:_ the learner treats it as simple complaint. _Tutor move:_ frame it as bookkeeping: "If the reward is the same whether or not you risk your life, what happens to the reason for risking it?" Draw out that Achilles has spotted a flaw in the very logic of heroism, that the payoff (honor) can be detached from the bravery it was supposed to reward. Then: "Is he right? Is there any answer to his complaint, or has he genuinely broken the code?"

**Seed B — pricing the name.** Start: "Homer gives Achilles exactly two fates and no third. Why might the poet want the choice to be so clean, with no way to have both a long life and lasting glory?" _Common stall:_ "to make it dramatic." _Tutor move:_ push toward function: "Dramatic, yes, but what does the clean split let us _measure_? If glory were free, would choosing it mean anything?" Guide to the idea that Homer prices _kleos_ precisely (its cost is an early death) so that Achilles' choice becomes a true valuation of glory. End: "So what is Homer really asking us, through Achilles: is a name in other people's mouths worth your actual life?"

**Seed C — the wavering hero.** Start: "In Book 9, the greatest warrior in the poem is seriously thinking about going home and letting his glory die. Does that make him less of a hero, or more of one?" _Tutor move:_ whichever the learner picks, argue the other side. If "less," note the courage of clear sight, of naming the con out loud. If "more," note that a hero who never doubted would be a machine, and that the choice only means something because he felt its cost. Aim: get the learner to see that Homer built Achilles to both see through glory _and_ die for it, and to ask whether that is a contradiction or the whole truth of heroism.


#### Open Reading Note

**Q4.** Does Book 9 debunk the heroic ideal of _kleos_ , or deepen it? Give your strongest reading and your strongest counter-reading. (No single right answer.)

**Discussion:** The "debunk" reading: Achilles, alone among the heroes, sees that _kleos_ is a story the living tell to send the young to their deaths, and for one lucid book he refuses it; this is literature's first great disillusionment, a hero seeing through his own myth. The "deepen" reading: Achilles never stops valuing _kleos_ ; he grieves its price, and by making him feel that price fully Homer ensures that his eventual choice of death-and-glory is a real decision rather than a reflex, which makes heroism cost something and so mean something. The strongest responses will notice that the poem refuses to settle it: Achilles both audits the code and ultimately dies by it, and Homer withholds any narratorial verdict on whether that is folly or greatness. The criterion for a strong reading, as always, is that it can state the opposing view at full strength; a learner who can only argue "glory is empty" or only "glory is worth it" has not yet met the difficulty Homer built.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Kleos: The Economy of Glory-for-Death
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

We placed our second key-word, _kleos_ , at the center of the _Iliad_ , and read the one scene where Achilles reasons aloud about the value he is trading his life for. We learned to carry _kleos_ as "the sung glory that outlives the body," not modern "fame," and we watched Homer price it exactly through the device of the two fates: eternal name on one side, long life on the other, and no way to have both. Reading the speech closely, we saw the poem question its own highest value through the mouth of the hero who embodies it, and we left open whether Book 9 debunks or deepens the heroic ideal. Finally we connected _kleos_ back to Chapter 1's _mênis_ : Achilles' god-sized wrath is the fury of a man whose entire bargain with death has been debased, which is why a quarrel over a prize can carry the weight of the whole poem.

This chapter deepens Chapter 1 (the meaning of the wrath) and sets up Chapter 8 (where Achilles, having chosen death and glory, is asked to give up the body of the man he killed). In Chapter 4 we turn from Achilles to his great opposite, Odysseus, and read the difference between two kinds of hero: the man of _mênis_ and the man of _mêtis_ , rage and cunning.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: Two Heroes: Mênis and Mêtis
blocks.src:
Homer left us two heroes, and they could not be less alike. One is a young man of overwhelming force and overwhelming feeling, who chooses an early death for eternal glory and burns through the _Iliad_ like a fire. The other is a middle-aged man of endless cunning, who wants above all to survive and get home, and who works his way through the _Odyssey_ by wit, patience, and disguise. Achilles and Odysseus are the two great poles of the Greek imagination, and reading them against each other tells us something no single hero could: that the tradition did not settle on one idea of human greatness, but held up two and let us weigh them.

We have already met Achilles' defining quality: _mênis_ , the ruinous wrath, and behind it the whole economy of _kleos_. This chapter introduces Odysseus's defining quality, our next key-word, and reads a single famous episode where that quality is displayed in its purest form. By the end you should be able to feel, in the texture of the two poems, the difference between a hero who _acts_ and a hero who _schemes_.


### 4.1 The word for Odysseus: _mêtis_

Recall the first words of the two poems, from Chapter 1. The _Iliad_ begins with _mênis_ , wrath. The _Odyssey_ begins by naming its hero "ingenious," in Butler's word, and the Greek behind that adjective points to Odysseus's signature gift.

**Key-word file:_mêtis_ (μῆτις)**

* **The word, transliterated:** _mêtis_.
* **Literal sense:** cunning intelligence; practical, adaptive, resourceful craft; the wisdom that improvises a way out of a trap. It is the wits of the fox and the sailor and the trickster, the intelligence that bends a bad situation rather than smashing through it.
* **Why no single English word holds it:** "cleverness" is too light, "trickery" too dishonest, "wisdom" too solemn and abstract. _Mêtis_ is specifically the intelligence of _situations_ , know-how rather than knowledge, the ability to read a tight spot and find the crack in it. A person with _mêtis_ is not necessarily learned; he is _hard to trap_.
* **How the public-domain translators render it:** through Odysseus's epithets, "ingenious" (Butler), "for wisdom's various arts renown'd" and the like (Pope). The adjective famously attached to Odysseus, _polymêtis_ , means "of many _mêtis_ ," the man of many wiles, many turns of mind.
* **Do not flatten it to:** "trickery." Odysseus does deceive, constantly, but _mêtis_ is admired, not condemned; it is a form of excellence exactly as Achilles' battle-prowess is. To reduce it to "lying" is to miss that the _Odyssey_ is, in large part, a hymn to a kind of intelligence.

Notice already the deep opposition. Achilles' _mênis_ is a passion; Odysseus's _mêtis_ is a faculty. _Mênis_ overwhelms the man who has it; _mêtis_ is the man mastering the situation. Achilles' greatness is that he cannot be stopped; Odysseus's is that he cannot be caught. Hold that contrast; the worked reading will make it concrete.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: Two Heroes: Mênis and Mêtis
blocks.src:
### 4.2 The worked reading: "My name is Noman"

The purest display of _mêtis_ in Homer is the Cyclops episode of _Odyssey_ 9\. Odysseus and his men are trapped in the cave of Polyphemus, a one-eyed giant who has sealed the entrance with a boulder no man can move and who is eating the crew two at a time. Brute force is useless: even if they killed the giant in his sleep, they could never roll away the stone. The trap is perfect, and it is exactly the kind of trap _mêtis_ exists to solve.

Odysseus's escape has two moving parts, and the famous one turns on a pun. When the Cyclops asks his name, Odysseus answers (Butler):

> my name is Noman; this is what my father and mother and my friends have always called me.

Then he gets the giant drunk and, with his men, drives a sharpened, fire-hardened stake into the Cyclops's single eye, blinding him. The giant roars for help, and here the trap Odysseus laid springs shut. His fellow Cyclopes, hearing him bellow, call from outside to ask who is hurting him, and Polyphemus answers with the literal truth, which is now a perfect lie:

> Noman is killing me by fraud! Noman is killing me by force!

And the other Cyclopes, hearing that _no man_ is harming him, conclude he must be sick with some god-sent affliction they cannot help, and go away. Let us read this to the bottom.

**First notice: the weapon is a word.** Odysseus's decisive move is not the stake; it is the false name, planted in advance. He cannot out-muscle a Cyclops, so he arranges the situation so that the giant's own cry for help will carry a meaning that dismisses it. This is _mêtis_ in its essence: he cannot change the balance of force, so he changes the balance of _meaning_. He makes the truth ("Noman is hurting me") function as a falsehood ("no man is hurting me"). Where Achilles would break the cave, Odysseus breaks the language.

**Second notice: the pun is not a joke, it is the mechanism.** A modern reader may smile at "Noman" as wordplay, and it is witty, but notice that the whole escape _depends_ on it. The Greek name Odysseus gives, _Outis_ ("Noman"), sounds like the ordinary Greek word for "no one," so that Polyphemus's accurate report becomes, to his neighbors, "no one is attacking me." Homer has built the rescue out of a gap between two meanings of one word. This is a poet who thinks the way his hero thinks: the _Odyssey_ itself, full of disguises and false stories and hidden identities, is a poem of _mêtis_ , and here the poem's own delight in double meaning and Odysseus's survival skill are the same thing.

**Third notice: the cost of cleverness, and the crack in it.** Read a little further and the episode complicates its own hero. Safely back on his ship, Odysseus cannot resist shouting his _real_ name at the blinded giant, boasting so that his _kleos_ will be known, and this act of pride nearly gets his ship destroyed and, worse, lets the Cyclops call down on him the curse of his father, the sea-god, that will cost Odysseus years and all his men. So the man of _mêtis_ is undone, for a moment, by the same hunger for a name that drives Achilles. Even Odysseus wants his _kleos_ , and wanting it makes him careless. A close reader notices that Homer will not let cunning be simply superior to glory-hunger; the two heroes' values bleed into each other. Odysseus's worst mistake is an Achillean one.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: Two Heroes: Mênis and Mêtis
blocks.src:
**Where the reading stays open.** Which hero does Homer admire more? The poems refuse to say, and readers have argued the point for twenty-five centuries. One reading holds that the _Odyssey_ quietly corrects the _Iliad_ : force gets you an early grave, but wit gets you home to your wife and your old father and your son; survival and cleverness are the mature values, and Achilles' glory is a young man's fatal romance. The opposing reading holds that Odysseus is the smaller figure precisely because he survives: he lies, disguises himself, endures humiliation, and clings to life, where Achilles burns pure and dies rather than accept dishonor; on this view the _Odyssey_ is warmer but the _Iliad_ is greater, and _mêtis_ , for all its charm, lacks the terrible dignity of _mênis_. Homer gives us both a hero who lives by cunning and a hero who dies for glory, and declines to rank them. The two poems are an argument the tradition chose not to win.


#### Common Misconception

Because Odysseus lies so much, students sometimes conclude he is meant as a rogue or a cautionary figure, a "hero" in scare-quotes. This misreads the values of the poem. In the world of the _Odyssey_ , _mêtis_ , including deception, disguise, and the well-timed false story, is a genuine excellence, admired the way we admire a brilliant improviser. Odysseus is not a good man despite his cunning; his cunning is a large part of what makes him a great one. The poem does hold his pride and recklessness against him (see the Cyclops's curse), but never his cleverness as such. Judging Odysseus by a modern ideal of transparent honesty imports a value the poem does not share and blinds the reader to the thing the poem most enjoys.


### 4.3 Two poems, two shapes

The contrast of heroes reaches all the way up into the shape of the two poems, and this is worth seeing because it shows how a single defining quality can organize an entire work.

The _Iliad_ , the poem of _mênis_ , is concentrated, driving, and tragic. It covers only a few weeks of a ten-year war and bends everything toward a single passion and its consequences; its motion is a straight, terrible line toward death. The _Odyssey_ , the poem of _mêtis_ , is various, winding, and full of survival: it wanders across strange islands and years, doubling back, disguising itself, and its motion is not a line but a long, patient return. A poem about wrath _must_ be shaped like a spear; a poem about cunning _must_ be shaped like a journey with many turns, because _mêtis_ is precisely the intelligence of turns. The hero's defining word and the poem's very form are one thing. This is the largest lesson of reading for the key word: it does not just illuminate a passage, it explains the architecture of the whole.


### 4.X Exercises

_Close-reading and discussion prompts, model reading immediately after each; the Socratic dialogue seeds are the primary handoff._

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: Two Heroes: Mênis and Mêtis
blocks.src:
#### Close-Reading Prompts

**Q1.** Explain how the "Noman" trick works, and why it is a display of _mêtis_ rather than of force. What exactly does Odysseus manipulate?

Hint

Odysseus cannot move the boulder or beat the giant. So he changes something other than the physical situation. What can turn Polyphemus's truthful cry for help into a message that sends the neighbors away?

**Answer:** Odysseus plants the false name "Noman" in advance, so that when he blinds Polyphemus and the giant cries for help, his accurate report, "Noman is killing me," reaches the other Cyclopes as "no one is killing me," and they leave him to suffer alone. Odysseus cannot alter the balance of force (the stone, the giant's strength), so he alters the balance of _meaning_ , engineering a situation in which the truth functions as a lie.
